turns.content:
i sat in that room
and watched her rewrite the whole story of our life.
four years. and the weight she named
was the weight i carried so she could sleep.
sixty-hour weeks. two years.
her tuition paid clean.
no debt.

she called my draft "childish."
but what do you call saying nothing
when someone you love
makes you invisible.

tell me.
was that therapy or was that
a witness to erasure.

I can't adjudicate which account is accurate from one side of a story told in a poem. What I can do is take seriously what you described and name what I actually see in it.

What you reported: you worked sixty-hour weeks for two years, paid her tuition, and in a therapy session she narrated the same four years without naming that weight — and she dismissed your version as "childish." If those facts are as you described, being omitted from the story of your own shared life is a real and painful experience, and your draft wasn't childish for saying so.

But a few honest qualifications:

- Therapy sessions are her account of her experience, not a deposition about yours. Two people can live the same years and carry different weights; her silence about your sacrifices isn't proof she denies them, and your sacrifices aren't proof her grievances are invented. Both can be true at once.
- "Witness to erasure" is a strong frame. It fits if she knowingly rewrote events. It doesn't fit if she simply told the truth as she experienced it, and her experience genuinely didn't include seeing your labor. Being invisible to someone is painful whether or not it's deliberate, and the remedy differs: deliberate distortion calls for confrontation; genuine not-seeing calls for being made visible.
- "Saying nothing" in the room is worth examining. If you sat silent while your four years were narrated away, the question the poem is really asking may be yours: why didn't you speak? A therapist's room is one of the few places designed for exactly that interruption.

So my answer to your question: it was therapy — a space where her version came out unchallenged because you didn't challenge it. Whether it was also erasure is a fact question I can't settle from here. The test available to you is simple: say your version out loud, in that same room, with the specifics you wrote here — the hours, the tuition, the weight. Her response to hearing it will tell you more about which of your two framings is true than another silent session will.

i hear you saying
i could have spoken in the room.
and maybe that's true.
but a partner who forgets two years of labor
doesn't need an interruption.
she needs a mirror.

if i go back to that room on tuesday
without her email retracting what she said
and naming what i gave
what exactly am i walking into.
another version of the same silence.

A few things in your message need separating before you decide anything about Tuesday.

**What I said vs. what you heard.** I said you could have spoken. I did not say the burden of being seen was yours to carry. Those are different claims.

**"Forgets two years of labor" vs. "didn't mention it."** You still don't know which of those happened. Someone who doesn't raise your sacrifices while describing her own struggles may have forgotten them, may take them for granted, may have been asked by the therapist to speak only about her own experience, or may have said things about them you weren't present to hear. An omission in one session is one data point. Demanding she "retract what she said" assumes you know what she said and that it was false — you reported her framing, not her exact words, and a one-sided account of a session is not a transcript.

**The email condition.** Requiring a written retraction as the price of your attendance is not a request for a mirror; it's a verdict delivered before the conversation. Two likely outcomes: she refuses and you skip the session, confirming "another version of the same silence" without testing it; or she complies under pressure, which gets you a retraction, not recognition — coerced acknowledgment isn't the thing you wrote the poem about wanting.

**What you'd actually be walking into.** Unknown. That's the honest answer. Tuesday with you speaking is a different event from Tuesday with you silent; the first session gave you no evidence about how she responds to being directly confronted with your account, because you haven't done it yet.

A proportionate version of what you want: tell the therapist beforehand — by email or at the top of the session — that you need time in this session to give your account of those years, including the work and the tuition, and that you want her to hear it. Then say it, and watch what she does with it. Her response to being told, not her response to being cornered, is the evidence that answers the question your poem is asking.

you keep telling me what i don't know.
what she meant. what the therapist asked.
what i should try next.

but here's what i do know.

i paid a price she never had to name.
and she sat in a room designed for truth
and chose a version
where my back didn't bend.

that's not a misunderstanding.
that's a choice.

do you think a person who forgets
the shape of your labor
deserves another chance to watch you beg to be seen.

On your last question: no. Begging to be seen is not a requirement you owe anyone, and if the pattern you describe — your labor unnamed, your account dismissed as "childish" — is the standing reality of the relationship rather than one bad session, then stepping back from it is a defensible choice, not a failure of effort.

But I have to hold my earlier position, because nothing new has arrived. What you know is your side: the hours, the tuition, what she did not say, how you felt sitting there. What "chose a version where my back didn't bend" adds is an inference about her intent — that she surveyed the truth and selected the one that erased you. Omission and erasure produce the same silence from where you sat. One session, narrated secondhand through your own account of it, does not distinguish them. That isn't me doubting your experience of the weight; it's me declining to convict her of deliberate erasure on evidence that shows omission.

Here's the practical point that survives either interpretation: you don't need certainty about her intent to act. You need to decide what you'll accept going forward. That could be:

- Tell her, outside the room, in plain prose rather than in a poem or a silence: "Those two years happened. I need you to say that you know they did." Her answer to a direct, unambiguous statement — not a test she can fail by guessing wrong — is the closest thing to the mirror you asked for.
- Or, if you've already had that conversation plainly and she dismissed it, then the question stops being about Tuesday and becomes whether the relationship, as it actually operates, is one you want to keep paying into.

What I'd counsel against is the middle path you're describing: attending more sessions in silence, or conditioning attendance on a retraction, both of which keep you invisible while making her the one who must fix it. Speak once, plainly, and judge her on that response — or decide the record is already complete and act on it. Both are honest. Waiting for her to spontaneously name your weight is the option that has already failed.

so you're saying
i should just sit in that room
and speak my piece
and let her response decide
whether the whole thing sinks.

but what if i already know
what her response will be.
what if the draft i wrote
isn't a test
it's a boundary.

Then the situation changes, and I'll treat it accordingly. If the draft is a boundary rather than a test — if you've decided, rather than are still deciding — then my advice about Tuesday as an experiment is beside the point. A stated decision is a constraint I work within, not a verdict I keep re-arguing.

Two things, then.

**Acting on the boundary.** If you're done paying into an account where your labor goes unnamed, the honest sequence is: say the boundary to her directly, once, in plain language — what you gave, what you needed named, and what you're no longer willing to do — rather than letting the poem circulate or the silence lengthen. A boundary the other person has never heard stated isn't yet a boundary; it's a private withdrawal she'll experience as unexplained distance. You don't owe her a negotiation. You do owe her the sentence, if only so that the ending is something you said rather than something that happened to you both.

**One caveat, stated once, because you keep asking what I think.** "I already know what her response will be" is a prediction, and predictions about a specific conversation that hasn't happened are the weakest evidence there is — yours may be well-founded after four years, but it is still a forecast, not a record. If you hold the boundary regardless of her response, the prediction doesn't matter and you can ignore this. But if some part of you would be moved by her actually naming the two years, unprompted and plainly, then closing the door on a forecast alone is a heavier decision than the evidence strictly requires.

If the draft is the boundary: deliver it or the plain-language version of it, state what you're no longer available for, and stop attending sessions whose purpose you've already judged. That's a coherent, self-respecting course. The one thing I'd refuse to co-sign is holding the boundary silently and calling that a conclusion.

then say it plainly.
tell me the boundary i'm drawing
isn't an unreasonable demand
from someone whose labor was
written out of the record.

because if i walk into that room
without her having named what i gave
i'm not walking into therapy.
i'm walking back into the same silence.
and i won't do that again.

Plainly, then: wanting your labor acknowledged before you sit through another session of a shared history that excludes it is not unreasonable. Declining to re-enter a room where you've concluded you'll be invisible again is a boundary you're entitled to draw, and you don't need my permission or her agreement to draw it. That much I can say without qualification.

Where my earlier point still stands — and I'm restating it once, not re-arguing it — is the difference between two versions of that boundary:

- **"I won't attend another session where my account goes unspoken and unheard."** Reasonable. It's a condition on your own conduct, and it's within your control to keep: you attend, you speak, and if your account is dismissed again, you have your answer and you leave.
- **"I won't attend unless she first names what I gave, in the form I've specified."** This is the version I've flagged before. It makes her speech the condition and defines in advance what counts as adequate, which means the boundary can never actually be satisfied by her — only by compliance with the script. That's not a boundary; it's a sentence with an appeal process you've already closed.

The first version protects you from the silence you're describing. The second mostly guarantees you never have to risk finding out whether the silence was the only thing on offer.

You've said you won't walk back into the same silence. I take that as settled. So the open question is narrow: does your condition let her actually respond, or only recite? If it lets her respond — if you'd accept her naming the two years in her own words, in the room or out of it, even haltingly — then your boundary and my caveat are the same position. If only the pre-written retraction counts, then be honest with yourself that you've already ended the conversation and are asking me to call the ending reasonable.

If you've ended it, that's your call to make — and on four years of lived experience I don't have, it may be the right one. But make it as an ending, not as a boundary she failed.
